description:
Exploring how microgravity affects flame behaviour and combustion using NASA’s experimental data. Our goal is to develop an interactive, AI-powered dashboard that analyses combustion patterns and presents useful insights for improving fire safety in space missions.

Open to curious minds who are interested in space science, Python, data analysis, AI/ML, web development and UI/UX design. Beginners who are eager to learn and contribute are welcome!
summary: I built Flame in Freefall: Combustion Investigation Explorer, a simple interactive app made with Python and Streamlit. It brings  NASA microgravity combustion investigations (currently  six) from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into one searchable view: ACME CLD Flame, SAFFIRE-I, II and III, a cool-flame simulation study, and ACME CFI-G. For each one, users can see the objective, approach, flight platform, DOI, license and sample-table rows, all shown as published by NASA. It addresses the challenge by making combustion research easier to explore, so researchers can quickly see what each investigation tested. This matters because spacecraft fire safety depends on understanding how flames behave in microgravity. It is a prototype for exploration, not an analysis of measurement data and not a validated safety tool.
details:
What it does and how it works
Flame in Freefall: Combustion Investigation Explorer is a small web app that lets a user browse NASA microgravity combustion investigations in one place. It currently covers six investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository: ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21), SAFFIRE-I, II and III (PSI-98, 99, 100), a cool-flame simulation study (PSI-117) and ACME CFI-G (PSI-159). Users can filter by investigation type, search by text, view a chart of the investigations, and open a details panel showing the objective, approach, flight platform, DOI, license and sample-table rows. I copied this information by hand from the PSI pages into two CSV files, and the app reads them with pandas and displays them with Streamlit and Plotly.

Benefits and intended impact
NASA’s combustion investigations are described on separate pages, so it is hard to compare what each one tested. The explorer gives researchers, students and engineers a quick overview and links each entry to its PSI source and DOI. The intended impact is to make combustion research easier to find and understand, which supports fire-safety research for future space missions.

Tools used
Python, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly, CSV files, GitHub, and a laptop. No special hardware was used. The code and README were written with help from Claude (Anthropic); the choice of challenge and data and the review of everything were mine. No SI runs inside the app.

Creativity and factors considered
The design is deliberately simple and transparent. Every value is shown exactly as published, and I flagged oddities in NASA’s tables, such as “037 mm” entries and differing length and width values, instead of quietly correcting them. I considered accuracy, licensing (the PSI pages show CC0-1.0), and the limited time available, so I included only data I could verify and made no claims I couldn’t support.

Limitations and next steps
This is a catalogue of what each investigation tested, not an analysis of the measurement files, and it is not a validated fire-safety tool. Future work would load the real measurement data, compare conditions across experiments, and add a clearly labelled language-model summary of related NASA papers.
